## Summary
The three enacted regimes are the EU AI Act, California’s SB 53 (the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act), and New York’s final RAISE Act. Each uses a strict **greater-than** training-compute threshold, but their consequences differ. The EU AI Act is the only one that makes crossing—or anticipating crossing—the threshold itself a direct regulatory-notification trigger. California and New York use the threshold chiefly to define the frontier models and developers subject to transparency, safety-framework, and incident-reporting requirements.

| Jurisdiction | Exact threshold | Legal instrument / provision | Mandatory reporting consequence | Effective date | Relative coverage of announced training runs |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| **European Union** | **More than 10^25 cumulative FLOPs** used to train a general-purpose AI (GPAI) model. The Commission may also designate a below-threshold model as systemic-risk based on its capabilities and impact. | **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act)**, Arts. **51(1)–(2)** (systemic-risk presumption/designation), **52(1)** (notification), and **55** (systemic-risk duties). | The provider must notify the European Commission **without delay and no later than two weeks** after the model meets the threshold, or after it knows the model is expected to meet it. Systemic-risk GPAI providers must also report serious incidents and satisfy evaluation, risk-management, and cybersecurity duties. | **2 August 2025** | **Broadest.** The threshold is one order of magnitude below the California and New York thresholds, and discretionary designation can reach certain lower-compute models. |
| **California** | **More than 10^26 FLOPs** to train a qualifying frontier foundation model. A **large frontier developer** has annual gross revenue above **$500 million**. | **California SB 53**, Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act, Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code **§§ 22757.11–22757.12**. | The threshold defines a frontier developer; it does not require a standalone notice that a training run has crossed it. Covered developers must publish pre-deployment transparency reports; large frontier developers must publish annual frontier-AI safety frameworks; critical safety incidents must be reported to the Office of Emergency Services. | **1 January 2026** | Narrower: only announced runs above **10^26 FLOPs** meet the model threshold. |
| **New York** | **More than 10^26 computational operations**—integer or floating-point—to train a frontier model. The final law also covers a model made through knowledge distillation from such a model. A **large frontier developer** has annual gross revenue above **$500 million**. | **New York Responsible AI Safety and Education (RAISE) Act**, N.Y. Gen. Bus. Law art. 44-B, especially **§ 1420** (definitions), as replaced by the final chapter amendment, **S8828/A9449**. | As in California, the threshold defines a frontier model/developer rather than triggering a separate training-run notice. Large frontier developers must establish, implement, and publish safety frameworks and report qualifying critical safety incidents to the State within **72 hours**; DFS has oversight and rulemaking responsibilities. | **1 January 2027** | Same nominal compute cutoff as California, but only for models developed, deployed, or operating in whole or part in New York. Academic research institutions are generally exempt. |

The finalized New York law **does not retain a $100 million training-compute-cost condition** in the frontier-model definition. That condition appeared in earlier enacted text, but the March 27, 2026 chapter amendment replaced it with California-aligned definitions: **more than 10^26 operations** for a frontier model and **more than $500 million in annual gross revenue** for a large frontier developer. The revenue figure determines which developers bear the core safety-framework and incident-reporting duties; it is not an additional compute threshold for a training run.

The **EU AI Act would capture the largest number of currently announced training runs**, as a threshold matter. Every run above California’s or New York’s **10^26** cutoff necessarily exceeds the EU’s **10^25-FLOP** cutoff, whereas runs above 10^25 but at or below 10^26 are within the EU presumption but outside both state-law model definitions. EU Commission designation of consequential lower-compute GPAI models broadens its potential coverage further.

Available public model-count evidence reinforces that conclusion, while cautioning against treating the counts as a census. Epoch AI estimated that, as of April 2025, approximately **30 publicly available models** had been trained above **10^25 FLOPs**, compared with only **two** above **10^26 FLOPs**. Its estimates rely on publicly announced “notable” models for which training compute can be estimated; actual counts may be higher, especially as frontier developers increasingly withhold training details. Epoch projects rapid growth in models above 10^26 FLOPs—roughly **30 notable models by the start of 2027** and **more than 200 by the start of 2030** in its median scenario—meaning that fixed numerical thresholds, particularly the EU’s lower one, may encompass substantially more models over time.

The resulting coverage ranking is therefore:

1. **EU AI Act:** >10^25 cumulative FLOPs, plus possible below-threshold systemic-risk designation;  
2. **California SB 53:** >10^26 FLOPs;  
3. **New York RAISE Act:** >10^26 operations, subject to New York nexus and—with respect to the core large-developer duties—>$500 million annual gross revenue.
